look_here_first: LOW, sprawling or mat-forming plant; leaves OPPOSITE, oval-to-triangular and shallowly toothed. Tiny YELLOW composite heads sit almost directly in the LEAF AXILS (where leaf meets stem). Confirm the Asteraceae head: short ray florets around yellow disc florets; inspect the green phyllaries beneath the head and, when mature, small awned cypselae. Do not identify by yellow flower color alone.

key_traits.label: Best field traits
key_traits.text: Creeping/procumbent perennial; delicate branched shoots spread through thin turf or along path edges and can root at nodes.; Leaves in opposite pairs, often rotated 90 degrees at successive nodes (decussate); one simple blade per petiole.; Leaf blades usually ovate, broadly lanceolate or somewhat triangular (deltate), about 1–3 cm commonly, sometimes larger; shallow rounded teeth on margins; three prominent veins arise near the base.; Single small yellow COMPOSITE head about 4–8 mm across, nearly stalkless (subsessile), nestled where a leaf meets the stem.; Small ray florets are present but have short yellow limbs; inner yellow disc florets are separate tiny flowers, not a single disc.; Beneath a head inspect a few green overlapping phyllaries (typically about 4–6), not ordinary flower sepals.; In fruit, look for flattened dry one-seeded cypselae with two conspicuous barbed awns (small additional awns may occur).

key_traits.label: Life cycle
key_traits.text: Perennial herb; can regrow from its established plant base and spreading branches. Flowering reported nearly year-round across its geographic range, but Central Texas flowering varies with rain, mowing and frost.

key_traits.label: Growth habit
key_traits.text: Prostrate to decumbent (trailing or partly lifted), branched herb, roughly 4–27 cm high and stems to about 40 cm long in the UT Williamson County treatment; sometimes forms loose mats among turf. Look for roots at contacting nodes, not tall vertical stalks.

key_traits.label: Stem
key_traits.text: Slender cylindrical green or sometimes red-striped/purplish stems, hairy with short, mostly upward-pointing stiff hairs (strigose), branching at nodes. Shoot tips can rise despite generally creeping habit.

key_traits.label: Leaf arrangement
key_traits.text: Opposite and decussate: leaves emerge in pairs from each node; successive pairs typically cross in orientation. Not alternate and not three leaflets.

key_traits.label: Leaves
key_traits.text: Simple, small, petiolate blades; ovate to deltate (triangular-ovate), sometimes broadly lanceolate; low crenate-serrate teeth, not smooth coin-shaped margins; short appressed hairs on both surfaces. Williamson County measured 6.5–54 mm long × less than 5–28 mm wide, with variation.

key_traits.label: Leaf venation
key_traits.text: Often three principal veins arising near the leaf base plus pinnate secondary venation. Veins assist confirmation but overlap with other small herbs; do not identify from three basal veins alone.

key_traits.label: Inflorescence
key_traits.text: Usually a solitary radiate CAPITULUM (flower head) at a leaf axil; heads very short-stalked or nearly stalkless (subsessile). A leafy branch may continue immediately beside the head, making the head seem part of a cluster.

key_traits.label: Heads
key_traits.text: Typically ~4–8 mm across. What looks like one tiny flower is a composite head of multiple separate yellow florets: short outer ray florets and central disc florets.

key_traits.label: Phyllaries
key_traits.text: Small overlapping green involucral bracts beneath the head, often 4–6; Williamson County describes a bell-shaped involucre ~5–6 mm long. These are crucial Asteraceae organs; not yet verified in existing gallery photos.

key_traits.label: Flower
key_traits.text: Yellow ray florets bear a short straplike corolla with lobes at the tip; central yellow disc florets are tubular and bisexual. Number and visibility vary; check with a hand lens rather than expecting a large showy daisy.

key_traits.label: Fruit
key_traits.text: Cypsela (dry one-seeded fruit, often called an achene), typically ~2–4 mm long; often flattened and sometimes somewhat angled, with usually two conspicuous spreading-to-ascending barbed awns of the pappus (smaller additional awns possible). Fruit angle is NOT invariably three-sided.

key_traits.label: Habitat
key_traits.text: Warm Central Texas lawns and lightly shaded turf margins, path edges, garden beds, roadsides and other disturbed ground; tolerates several soil types including clays and calcareous soils. Habitat is supporting, not an ID character.

key_traits.label: Field season
key_traits.text: In Central Texas, look for leaves and spreading runners across much of the growing season, tiny heads during warm or moist spells; flowering may pause in dry or freezing weather. FNA reports flowering approximately year-round geographically; do not promise year-round local blooms.

key_traits.label: Measurement tip
key_traits.text: Flower head ~4–8 mm across, far smaller than most conspicuous daisies. Carry a 1 mm-rule/hand lens for phyllaries and small awned fruit.

key_traits.label: Key cautions
key_traits.text: Low stature plus yellow color is insufficient. Opposite leaves and short yellow rays are shared with other herbs; the almost stalkless axillary capitulum and reproductive microstructure are strongest checks. A 3-angled cypsela is possible but not universal.

names: Synedrella nodiflora (introduced tropical comparison; not assumed locally frequent)
lookalikes.differences: Frogfruit: tiny white/pink flowers crowded into a button/cylinder on a noticeable naked axillary stalk, rather than a yellow ray-and-disc composite head. Carolina ponyfoot: round or kidney-shaped, entire-margined ALTERNATE leaves on long petioles, and minute non-daisy flowers. False daisy (Eclipta): opposite but much narrower/larger leaves; many short WHITE ray florets in a larger head, often wetter habitats. Hairy wedelia: much larger yellow/orange flower heads on longer peduncles and taller, coarse, often woody-based stems. Synedrella nodiflora: a useful botanical comparison in introduced floras, more erect with clustered heads; local occurrence should be checked before making it a core Hays field target.
